questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
questions.title: JavaScript closures
questions.direct_answer: A closure is the combination of a function and the lexical environment in which that function was created. It lets the function keep accessing outer variables after the outer call has finished, because the needed bindings remain reachable through the returned or stored function.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether closures are explained through lexical bindings and lifetime.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling a closure a frozen copy of every outer value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connecting useful private state with retention costs.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Every function is created with access to its lexical environment.
A returned callback can keep outer bindings reachable after the outer call returns.
Closures capture bindings, not frozen copies of their current values.
Separate factory calls create separate environments.
Long-lived closures can also retain large objects longer than intended.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A closure is a function together with access to the lexical bindings around the place where the function was defined. That access is based on source location, not on where the function is later called.

For example, `makeCounter` can declare a private `count` variable and return a function that increments it. The outer call finishes, but the returned function still reaches that particular count binding. Calling `makeCounter` again creates a separate binding and therefore an independent counter.

The captured item is a live binding rather than a snapshot. If code in the same environment changes the variable, the closure sees the new value. This explains both useful state and common loop bugs when several callbacks share one `var` binding.

Closures power callbacks, factories, module privacy, memoization, and partial application. Their boundary is lifetime: as long as a reachable function needs an outer environment, values reachable through that environment cannot be collected. I keep captured state small and expose explicit cleanup when a long-lived callback also owns external resources.

sections.title: Lexical scope survives through reachability
sections.content: Returning from a function removes its normal stack frame, but it does not erase bindings still needed by a reachable inner function. The engine keeps the required environment available.

sections.title: Bindings belong to an environment, not to function source text
sections.content:
A function factory creates a fresh lexical environment on every call. Functions returned from the same call share its bindings; functions returned from different calls do not. This makes it possible to expose several operations over one private state object.

A closure does not automatically copy everything in scope. Engines may optimize what is retained, but application reasoning should focus on which outer values the callback references and how long that callback remains reachable.

questions.question: How can closures create private state?
questions.title: Private state with closures
questions.direct_answer: A factory function can declare state in its local scope and return selected functions that read or change it. Callers receive those functions but no direct reference to the binding, creating encapsulation. This privacy is per factory call and should be balanced against class fields or module-level state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether closure privacy is tied to an intentional public API.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning the mutable state object and calling it private.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Comparing factories with private fields and module scope.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Keep the state in a factory's local lexical environment.
Return only the operations that should access that state.
Each factory call receives independent private bindings.
The state lives as long as an exposed closure remains reachable.
Use private class fields when identity, inheritance, or many instances make a class clearer.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Closures provide privacy by putting a binding inside a factory and exposing functions rather than the binding itself. Outside code cannot name that local variable, but the returned functions still reach it through lexical scope.

For example, a balance factory can return `deposit` and `readBalance`. Both functions share one private `balance`, while callers cannot assign to it directly. A second factory call creates a different balance environment.

This is useful for small capability-based APIs, configuration, and stateful callbacks because the public surface can expose exactly the allowed operations. The functions can validate every change and preserve invariants before updating state.

The trade-off is that every instance creates function objects and retains its environment. A class with `#privateField` may be clearer when the object has many methods, needs a familiar instance shape, or shares methods through a prototype. Module scope is better for one shared singleton. I choose the form that makes ownership and lifetime easiest to understand.

sections.title: Privacy comes from not exporting the binding
sections.content: The outer variable is not magically hidden by a keyword. It is unreachable by name from callers because it belongs to another lexical environment; only the returned operations retain access.

sections.title: Capabilities can be narrower than object access
sections.content:
Returning one function gives the caller one capability. A read-only consumer can receive `get`, while a privileged consumer also receives `set`. This is stronger than returning a mutable object and relying on convention.

Privacy does not encrypt data or protect it from code that already owns a powerful closure. Debuggers may inspect environments. The benefit is application-level encapsulation and a smaller API contract.

questions.question: Why can closures inside loops produce unexpected values?
questions.title: Closures in loops
questions.direct_answer: Callbacks created in a loop with var share the loop's single function-scoped binding, so they read its final value when they run later. A let loop declaration creates a fresh binding for each iteration, giving each closure the expected value. A factory parameter can also create a per-call binding.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether closures are understood as access to live bindings.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Blaming timers without explaining the shared var binding.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguishing binding capture from shared object mutation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: var gives all loop callbacks one shared binding.
Callbacks read that binding when they execute, not when they are created.
A let loop declaration creates a fresh binding for each iteration.
A factory call can create an equivalent per-callback binding.
The same live-binding rule applies beyond timers to handlers and promises.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The classic loop issue happens because closures capture a binding, not a snapshot. A `for` loop declared with `var i` has one function-scoped `i`, and every callback created by the loop refers to that same binding.

For example, three timers scheduled during `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)` run after the loop and all print `3`, the value left when the loop ended. The timers are asynchronous, but the underlying cause is the shared binding.

A `for` loop with `let i` creates a new iteration binding. Each callback closes over its own binding and prints `0`, `1`, and `2`. Before `let`, a common solution was calling a factory or immediately invoked function with the current value as a parameter.

The boundary is that changing `var` to `let` fixes this binding problem, not every async ordering problem. A callback may still observe a shared object that other code mutates. I identify exactly which binding or object is shared before choosing the fix.

sections.title: Creation time and execution time are different
sections.content: A callback stores access to an environment when it is created. It reads a binding's current value when it later runs, so shared mutable bindings reveal changes made in between.

sections.title: Per-iteration binding is specified behaviour
sections.content:
For `for` loops using a lexical declaration, JavaScript creates a new environment for each iteration and initializes it from the previous value before executing the body. This is why closures receive distinct values without an extra factory.

`forEach` also provides each callback invocation with a parameter binding, so a callback nested inside that invocation can capture the parameter. The choice between constructs should still consider control flow such as break and await.

sections.title: Which binding does each callback see?
sections.content:
| Loop declaration | Bindings created | Later callback outputs |
|---|---|---|
| `var i` | One shared `i` | final value, final value, final value |
| `let i` | One per iteration | 0, 1, 2 |
